title: Demonstrate an understanding of propagation of deciduous fruit trees on a commercial scale

lessons.title: Rootstocks, cultivars and why we graft
lessons.html:
What is propagation?

Propagation means making new plants. In a commercial fruit tree nursery, thousands of young apple, pear, peach, plum and apricot trees are grown every year for farmers.

Why not just plant seeds?

If you plant a seed from a good apple, the new tree will not be the same as the parent. Its fruit could be small or sour. To get exactly the same fruit every time, nurseries use vegetative propagation: they take a piece of a good tree and join it onto another plant.

Two parts of a fruit tree

PartWhat it isWhat it gives
RootstockThe bottom part with the rootsStrong roots, size control, resistance to some soil pests and diseases, suited to the soil
Scion (cultivar)The top part that grows into the treeThe fruit type, for example a known apple or plum cultivar

The place where they are joined is the graft union. The rootstock and scion must be compatible, or the union will be weak.

Healthy material

Nurseries must use clean, healthy, true-to-type material. In South Africa, deciduous fruit nurseries usually work with certified material from registered mother blocks, so that viruses and diseases are not spread to farms. Never take cuttings or buds from any tree without permission, and never bring plant material from outside the nursery.

Growing rootstocks

Rootstocks can be grown from seed (for example peach seedling rootstocks) or from clonal methods such as layering in stool beds or rooting cuttings. They are planted in nursery rows and grown until they are thick enough to graft or bud.

lessons.title: Budding, grafting and nursery work
lessons.html:
Joining scion and rootstock

There are two main ways to join the cultivar to the rootstock.

Budding

A single bud is cut from a budstick of the cultivar and inserted under the bark of the rootstock. The common method is the T-bud or chip bud. It is usually done in summer or autumn when the bark slips easily or the plant is actively growing. The bud is tied in firmly with budding tape. After the bud has taken, the rootstock top is cut off above the bud so all growth goes into the new shoot.

Grafting

A piece of stem with several buds (a scion) is joined to the rootstock, usually in late winter while plants are dormant. Common methods are whip-and-tongue and cleft grafting. The cut surfaces of both parts must fit closely so the cambium (the thin green growing layer under the bark) of each touches. The join is then wrapped tightly.

Rules for success

  • Use a very sharp, clean knife. Clean cuts heal well.
  • Work fast so cut surfaces do not dry out.
  • Keep the cambium layers lined up.
  • Wrap firmly and label each row with cultivar and rootstock.
  • Disinfect tools between batches if instructed, to avoid spreading disease.

Nursery care

After budding or grafting, workers remove suckers from the rootstock, stake and tie the new shoots, irrigate, control weeds and watch for pests. In winter, trees are lifted, graded by size, counted, labelled and bundled for sale.

Safety

Budding knives are very sharp. Always cut away from your body and fingers, keep the knife closed or in its cover when not in use, and report cuts.

Key points

  • Fruit trees are propagated by joining a cultivar (scion) onto a rootstock.
  • Seeds do not give true-to-type fruit trees.
  • Budding uses a single bud; grafting uses a piece of stem with several buds.
  • The cambium layers must meet for the join to grow.
  • Use clean, certified material and label every row.
